preamble: Eight solutions, including all the longest, preceded one from Collins (but see also 11) and their clues lack definition.

clue.text: This car's just pressure in a new form

indicators.note: something put into a new form keeps its substance but takes a different shape, so the letters get rearranged

parts.note: the twenty letters of these words, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A motorist insists their vehicle is simply pressure given a fresh form.
explanation.walkthrough: The preamble says the themed answers have no definition; they are the musicals of Andrew Lloyd Webber, which came before The Woman in White, based on a Wilkie Collins novel.
explanation.definitionFit: This rock opera by Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice is one of the eight shows the preamble leaves undefined.

clue.text: Sweetheart's letter writing a greeting to Samuel with a verve: Sherlock (another name for Colin) is in time for fancy paintwork

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece is held within the surrounding letters

parts.note: jo is a Scots word for sweetheart, plus the possessive s
Ep. is the abbreviation for epistle, a letter
a hand is a person's style of handwriting
hi is a greeting
Sam is the short form of Samuel
zing means verve, energy, so a verve is a zing
tec is slang for a detective, and Sherlock Holmes is the most famous
an hour is a unit of time
Colin began as a pet form of Nicol, the Scots form of Nicholas
a fancy is a daydream
a coat is a layer of paint

explanation.surface: A love letter greets Samuel with gusto, then wanders into a detective, a man named Colin and some decorative painting.
explanation.walkthrough: A forty-letter title spread across four lights. Jo is Scots for sweetheart, and Colin began as a pet form of the Scots name Nicol. No word of the clue defines the show; the preamble does.
explanation.definitionFit: Lloyd Webber and Rice's early musical about the Biblical son of Jacob is one of the eight shows the preamble leaves undefined.

clue.text: At the end of the day a singular French game's very difficult, as they say

parts.words: At the end of the day
parts.note: sunset comes at the close of the day
boules is the French bowls game; singular makes it boule
v is the abbreviation for very
hard with its h dropped, as in a Cockney accent

explanation.surface: As evening falls, someone grumbles in a broad accent that a French game is very tough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As they say' points to the dropped-h pronunciation of hard, giving ARD. Boules is played with metal balls on gravel; one ball is a boule.
explanation.definitionFit: Lloyd Webber's musical of the Billy Wilder film about a faded silent star is one of the eight shows the preamble leaves undefined.

clue.text: Dog exactly like the last

parts.note: someone exactly like another is their dead spit, or spitting image
Z is the last letter of the alphabet

explanation.surface: A dog looks exactly like the one before it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The last' reads as the previous dog, but it is the last letter of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: The spitz is a breed type of dog with a pointed muzzle, pricked ears and a curled tail, such as the Pomeranian.

clue.text: Some big beasts swallowed by fish with no colour

indicators.note: what is swallowed ends up inside the swallower, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: huss is a dogfish, sold in Britain as rock salmon
the first part of elephants

explanation.surface: A fish has swallowed some large animals and lost all its colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' takes only the opening letters of the big beasts, elephants. Huss is a British fishmonger's name for dogfish.
explanation.definitionFit: A hue is a colour or shade, so lacking any hue means being colourless, an old and rare adjective.

clue.text: Sticker left off, take a pew during solver's return with 36

indicators.note: something left off is not included, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: a limpet sticks fast to rocks
L is the abbreviation for left

indicators.note: something happening during something else lies within it, so one piece sits inside the other
to return is to go back the way one came, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: the solver is addressed as you
take a pew is British slang for sit down

explanation.surface: A limpet comes away and the solver is asked to sit down.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a cross-reference: 36-across is HASTE. 'Take a pew' is British slang for sitting down, a pew being a church bench.
explanation.definitionFit: Impetuosity means rash eagerness, acting without thought, which is close to haste in the sense of hurried impatience.

clue.text: See 25 across
Still hungry? Attain and use organisation

indicators.note: organisation is putting things into a new order, so the letters are arranged afresh

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice to someone still hungry: get there and use some planning.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as a description rather than a dictionary synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Unsatiate is an old word for not satisfied, so someone not yet full after eating fits the description.

clue.text: She rises in 21

indicators.note: being in something means lying inside it, so the letters sit within a longer word
in a down entry, rising means reading from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: 21-down is NEOCONSERVATIVE, whose last five letters are taken

explanation.surface: A woman climbs within a right-wing movement.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit at the end of the answer to 21-down, read upwards. 'She' is not a definition: the preamble defines the theme answers.
explanation.definitionFit: Lloyd Webber and Rice's musical about Eva Perón of Argentina is one of the eight shows the preamble leaves undefined.

clue.text: Nameless bird with the odd numbered papers

indicators.note: without a name means losing the abbreviation for name, a single letter

parts.note: a starling is a common bird
the two letters where these words meet
a British daily paper, named for speed

explanation.surface: An anonymous bird keeps company with oddly numbered newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: N, for name, goes from STARLING. 'Odd numbered papers' also hints that the first and third words of STAR LIGHT EXPRESS are both newspaper titles, the Star and the Express.
explanation.definitionFit: Lloyd Webber's roller-skating musical about racing trains is one of the eight shows the preamble leaves undefined.

clue.text: Having wings — a thousand on the clock

parts.note: alar is an adjective meaning of or having wings
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

explanation.surface: Time flies: a winged clock shows a thousand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' means the thousand is added after the winged word. The definition is loose: an alarm is short for an alarm clock.
explanation.definitionFit: An alarm is a common short form for an alarm clock, the bedside timepiece that rings to wake a sleeper.

clue.text: Odd man out here, being potty — barking?

parts.note: jerry is British slang for a chamber pot
a springer spaniel is a dog, and dogs bark

explanation.surface: A misfit here is declared both potty and barking, two British words for mad.
explanation.walkthrough: Potty and barking both look like 'crazy', but one is a pot and the other a dog. The preamble's 'see also 11' flags this as the theme's exception.
explanation.definitionFit: Jerry Springer: The Opera was a stage musical not by Lloyd Webber, so it is the single outsider among this grid's shows.

clue.text: Moslem's local American reverse

indicators.note: to reverse is to go backwards, so the letters are read from right to left

parts.note: a local is a British pub, and an inn is one
US is short for American

explanation.surface: A Muslim's neighbourhood American goes into reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moslem's' reads as a possessive but is 'Moslem is'. A local is the pub nearest home.
explanation.definitionFit: A Sunni is a follower of the larger of the two main branches of Islam, so a Muslim of that tradition.

clue.text: See 9
Setter's a friend in maybe 12 office

parts.note: the setter speaking of himself says I'm
taken as written
a mate is a friend

explanation.surface: The setter says he has a friend in the office of a Muslim, perhaps a Sunni.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter's' means 'the setter is', so I'M. 12-across is SUNNI, and 'maybe' marks it as one example of the religion.
explanation.definitionFit: An imam leads prayer in a mosque, and the imamate is the rank or office of such a religious leader.

clue.text: What do you want for Christmas (before starting snoring, that is)?

definitions.text: What do you want for Christmas
definitions.note: a question whose answer is the noun

parts.note: pre- is the prefix meaning before
zz is the cartoon sound of someone starting to snore
i.e. is the abbreviation for id est, that is

explanation.surface: Someone asks what you want for Christmas, just before you nod off.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket looks like an aside, but it holds the whole wordplay. Prezzie is British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: A prezzie is a colloquial British word for a present, the usual reply to a question about Christmas wishes.

clue.text: Two points each, one short of wanting to drink the lot

indicators.note: being one short means a single letter is missing from the word that follows

parts.note: a thirsty person wants a drink
the lot means everything, all

explanation.surface: Two people each score twice, but one of them can't quite finish the drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The letter dropped is the S. In tennis the second point won in a game is called thirty.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis scoring the second point in a game is thirty, so a tied score of two points apiece is called thirty-all.

clue.text: Not 44 to deface

wordplay.note: 44-across is LONG MARCH; a march that is not long is the short form, the month abbreviation

explanation.surface: A cross-reference instruction: do not use 44 to spoil something.
explanation.walkthrough: 44-across is LONG MARCH; 'not long' March is the short March, Mar, the calendar abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: To mar is to spoil the look of something, to damage or disfigure it, which is what defacing does.

clue.text: Singlestick operator supports logophile

parts.note: to back is to support
a logophile is a lover of words, a word man

explanation.surface: A man who fences with a single stick is backed by a lover of words.
explanation.walkthrough: Singlestick is fencing with a wooden stick, and a backsword was the single-edged sword it imitates.
explanation.definitionFit: A backswordman fights with a backsword or with the singlestick, the wooden practice weapon used in place of one.

clue.text: Universities now

parts.note: surface reading: places that are universities today
setter's reading: Colleges of Advanced Technology, abbreviated, were raised to university status in the 1960s

explanation.walkthrough: Several British Colleges of Advanced Technology, known by their initials, became universities in the 1960s; the plural of those initials spells the themed show.
explanation.definitionFit: Lloyd Webber's long-running musical based on T. S. Eliot's poems is one of the eight shows the preamble leaves undefined.

clue.text: Spies a loo

parts.note: taken as written
the gents is a British name for a men's toilet

explanation.surface: Someone spots a toilet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spies' looks like a verb, as in spots, but it is the plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Agents are people employed by a secret service to gather intelligence, the usual sense of spies.

clue.text: Right wing today gives veterans no voice

indicators.note: something that gives yields and bends out of shape, so the letters lose their order

parts.note: the fifteen letters of these words

explanation.surface: Today's political right silences old soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gives' looks like a link meaning results in, but it signals the rearrangement.

clue.text: See 1
How big is the book?

definitions.note: a question whose answer is the noun
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the amount of space a thing takes up
second meaning: a single bound book

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a question about page count; the answer is both the measure of size and the bound book itself.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both the space something occupies, its size, and a single tome, as in one of a set.

clue.text: Aged relative of Katharina until tamed

indicators.note: something tamed is kept in check and held in, so the letters are confined within the words

parts.note: the letters run across the join of these two words

explanation.definitionFit: Naunt is an obsolete form of aunt, so an old word for a female relative, the sister of a parent.

clue.text: Airborne seeds, first changed, end with dispersal

parts.note: the fluff that carries a thistle's seeds through the air

clue.text: Reportedly on good terms with urban horticulturalists?

clue.text: Exponent of spin as curate in play

parts.note: a spinning top is all about spin
taken as written

clue.text: Perform better than gold in the open

clue.text: Errant aristocrat called immediately

explanation.walkthrough: Toff is British slang for a posh person, an aristocrat.

clue.text: Average sort of go-between

clue.text: Did Pecksniff employ him to steal?

clue.text: Communist achievement postponing fools' day?

clue.text: Mobile number partly in Greek I assume

clue.text: Time lost by Italian city firm taking water from Venezuela

clue.text: Turn up another card trick
